items.title: Deloitte tops new SEC audit client wins in a slow third quarter
items.summary: Deloitte picked up the most new SEC audit clients in the third quarter, in a quarter with only 110 new SEC engagements across the market, the lowest quarterly count since 2021.
detail: Accounting Today reported on 25 November that Deloitte led all firms for new SEC audit clients in Q3 2026.
Total new SEC engagements came to 110 for the quarter, the lowest quarterly volume since 2021, which points to fewer auditor switches and fewer new registrants.
Deloitte was already the largest SEC auditor by client count, with 926 SEC registrant clients in 2025, about 15% of the market, according to Ideagen Audit Analytics.
items.why: Auditor switching data is a practical window into audit market concentration, a recurring theme in audit regulation debates.

items.title: ASAF meets in London on 30 November and 1 December
items.summary: The IFRS Foundation has released the agenda and papers for the Accounting Standards Advisory Forum meeting in London on 30 November and 1 December 2026.
detail: The Accounting Standards Advisory Forum (ASAF) brings national and regional standard setters together with the IASB to give technical advice on its projects.

The meeting follows the IASB's 17 to 19 November board meeting, where the Board added narrow-scope projects on cryptoassets and targeted improvements to IFRS 16 and agreed to start the IFRS 17 post-implementation review in 2027.
items.why: ASAF is where standard setters such as the AASB and DSAK IAI feed national views into IFRS projects that later flow into AASB standards and PSAK.

items.title: Australian inflation jumps to 4.9%, its highest since 2023
items.summary: Annual CPI rose to 4.9% in October from 4.3% in September, above forecasts, and trimmed mean inflation rose to 3.8%, two weeks before the RBA's December meeting.
detail: The ABS monthly CPI released on 25 November showed headline inflation at 4.9% for the year to October, up from 4.3% in September and above the roughly 4.8% consensus. The RBA's preferred trimmed mean measure rose to 3.8% from 3.6%.
Energy and transport drove the rise, with automotive fuel up 32.5% over the year and housing costs up 6.4%.

The RBA cash rate is 4.85% after its fifth increase this year on 3 November. Commentators mostly expect a hold at the 7 to 8 December meeting with further hikes not ruled out. The ASX 200 fell 0.4% to 8,692 on the day.
items.why: A second inflation shock in Australia keeps the RBA tightening story alive and feeds straight into AUD and bond valuations.

items.title: US PCE inflation rises to 3.8% and cements a December Fed hike
items.summary: The Fed's preferred inflation gauge rose to 3.8% a year in October, with core PCE at 3.3%, above the 3.2% forecast, and markets now fully price a quarter-point hike on 8 to 9 December.
detail: Headline PCE prices rose 0.3% in October and 3.8% from a year earlier, up from 3.6% in September and the highest annual rate in about five months.
Core PCE rose 3.3% year on year against expectations of 3.2%. Because the 2025 government shutdown left CPI without an annual October rate, PCE is the main clean annual read for the month.
The Fed held its target range at 3.75% to 4.00% in October. Treasury yields still fell on the day, with the 10-year near 4.82% to 4.88%, as investors bought bonds during a tech sell-off.
items.why: A Fed hiking cycle with inflation near 4% affects discount rates, impairment testing and fair value measurement across IFRS reporters.

items.title: US proposes new Section 301 tariffs on 14 trading partners
items.summary: The Trump administration proposed new tariffs on China, the EU, Japan and 11 other economies under Section 301, replacing the broad tariffs struck down by the Supreme Court earlier this year.
detail: The administration said the 14 economies helped spur an influx of low-priced goods that undercut American companies. The tariffs are targeted and vary by economy.
Reported rates go up to 20%, with China facing 20% and the EU, South Korea and Japan around 15%, in line with deals negotiated in recent months.
USTR Jamieson Greer said the tariffs are unlikely to take effect for months. China disputed the allegations, and the US-China trade truce expires on 10 January.
items.why: Tariff changes feed into customs valuation, transfer pricing of cross-border goods and inflation forecasts used by central banks.

items.title: Chip stocks keep falling as Wall Street slides
items.summary: US stocks fell on Wednesday as the chip sell-off continued, with the S&P 500 down about 1.1% and the Nasdaq about 1.9% during the session.
detail: Yahoo Finance's live coverage put the S&P 500 down 1.1% and the Nasdaq Composite down 1.9% during the 25 November session, with the Dow near flat. Final closing figures were not yet available.
Reports pointed to weak guidance from Analog Devices, an unwinding of the AI trade, the new tariff proposals and the hotter core inflation reading.
On Tuesday the Dow closed at 50,018.70, up 0.85%, while the Nasdaq fell 1.48% to 23,733.54 and the S&P 500 fell 0.5% to 7,201.09.
items.why: Volatile tech valuations matter for goodwill impairment, share-based payment measurement and fair value disclosures this reporting season.

items.title: Greens back Labor's 30% minimum tax on discretionary trusts
items.summary: The Albanese government secured Greens support for a minimum 30% tax on some discretionary trusts from 2029-30, in exchange for raising private jet fuel excise to the motorist rate.
detail: The trust measure sets a minimum 30% tax on some discretionary trusts from 2029-30 and is projected to raise A$4.5 billion in its first year. Business groups had warned of a A$1 billion hit to small businesses.

Under the deal, fuel excise for private jets rises from 3.56 cents to 53.7 cents a litre, matching ordinary motorists. The ATO also gets extra resources to scrutinise trust distributions to charities and similar bodies, and pensioners are carved out of private health insurance rebate cuts.

Opposition leader Angus Taylor called it a "dirty deal" aimed at small business. The Greens had sought to close a loophole for non-taxpaying entities such as private schools and sporting clubs, but that change was left out.
items.why: A major change to Australian trust taxation that will shape tax planning for family groups and private businesses.

items.title: UN releases revised drafts of its tax convention and disputes protocol
items.summary: The UN published revised drafts of the Framework Convention on International Tax Cooperation and the Protocol on the Prevention and Resolution of Tax Disputes on 16 November, ahead of the sixth negotiating session in Nairobi from 30 November.
detail: According to EY, the revised disputes protocol redrafts provisions on advance pricing arrangements, advance rulings outside transfer pricing, cooperative compliance arrangements and mutual agreement procedure rules.

The first drafts of the convention and two early protocols, on cross-border services and on tax disputes, came out in July 2026. PwC notes that major differences remain over taxing rights, with some countries wanting the framework to complement existing treaties and others wanting it to change treaty outcomes.
items.why: The UN track could create a parallel to the OECD's MAP and APA framework, which matters for anyone studying tax dispute resolution.

items.title: Treaty round-up: Andorra ratifies Bulgaria DTA, Rwanda and Denmark start talks
items.summary: Andorra enacted legislation on 17 November to ratify its tax treaty with Bulgaria, and Rwanda and Denmark agreed to open negotiations on a double tax agreement.
detail: The weekly treaty round-up dated 25 November also said Japan's foreign ministry announced the signing of a replacement treaty with the Czech Republic on 24 November. The two sides agreed the text in principle in March 2026 and the Czech government approved signing in October; the new treaty will replace the 1977 treaty with former Czechoslovakia once ratified.
items.why: Treaty network changes show how countries keep updating bilateral rules while the multilateral debates continue.

items.title: Rupiah closes at a record low of Rp18,332
items.summary: The rupiah fell 0.56% to Rp18,332 per US dollar on Wednesday, its weakest close on record and the second-worst performance in Asia that day.
detail: The currency lost 102 points in the session. CNBC Indonesia, using Refinitiv data, had it at Rp18,310 in the afternoon and also called that the weakest level ever.

Analysts quoted by Suara.com linked the drop to Bank Indonesia signalling it does not expect to raise the BI-Rate further next year, keeping it at 6%. Liputan6 also pointed to MSCI's possible reclassification of Indonesia, which investors fear could trigger capital outflows.
Antara cited a forecast range of Rp18,330 to Rp18,400 for Thursday.
items.why: A record-weak rupiah raises foreign currency translation losses under PSAK 221 and lifts the rupiah value of USD-denominated tax bases.

items.title: IHSG drops 0.84% to 5,197.61 with nine of 11 sectors lower
items.summary: The Jakarta Composite fell 43.97 points to 5,197.61 on Wednesday as the rupiah weakened, with decliners outnumbering gainers by more than two to one.
detail: The index opened at 5,235.83 and traded between 5,165.67 and 5,246.79. Some 194 stocks rose, 453 fell and 187 were unchanged, with turnover of about Rp7.08 trillion.
Nine of the 11 sector indices fell. ISAT (−6.95%), BRPT (−6.62%) and WIFI (−5.75%) were the worst performers in the LQ45, according to Kontan.
items.why: Ongoing weakness on the IDX feeds fair value measurements for Indonesian listed investments and the MSCI reclassification debate.

items.title: MSCI denies it has softened its Indonesia downgrade plan
items.summary: MSCI said on 24 November there has been no change to its proposal to move Indonesia from emerging to standalone market status, rejecting a report that its CEO signalled openness to alternatives.
detail: MSCI opened its consultation on 15 October, proposing to move Indonesia's indexes from Emerging Market to Standalone Market status. The consultation runs to 30 April, with a decision due on or before 30 June.

MSCI called the report about its CEO's talks with President Prabowo "incorrect" and said it expects to proceed unless there is clear evidence of material improvements in governance and market functioning.
items.why: Index reclassification is a live case study in how market governance and disclosure quality affect the cost of capital.

items.title: OJK issues POJK 18 and 19 on insurer solvency and reporting integrity
items.summary: OJK issued POJK 18/2026 on insurer and reinsurer solvency, aligned with PSAK 117, and POJK 19/2026 on the integrity of financial reporting for insurers, guarantee institutions and pension funds.
detail: POJK 18/2026, announced on 21 November, sets a minimum solvency ratio of 120% and requires insurers designated as Domestic Systemically Important Insurers (D-SII) to hold an extra capital buffer of 15% of the minimum risk-based capital. OJK said it aligns the solvency framework with PSAK 117 Insurance Contracts, in force since 1 January 2025.

POJK 19/2026, announced on 23 November, covers financial reporting integrity in the insurance, guarantee and pension fund sectors. The draft version aimed to strengthen governance and internal controls over financial reporting.
items.why: These rules link PSAK 117 directly to prudential capital and bring internal control over financial reporting into Indonesian insurance regulation.

worth.title: Greens back Labor's 30% minimum tax on discretionary trusts
worth.text: A rare structural change to Australian trust taxation, with a clear policy trade-off and real planning consequences for private groups.
